exposure to blue enriched polychromatic light during the evening impacts upon homeostasis, as indexed by reduced slow wave activity, and that the effects are particularly pronounced in the frontal region.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the impact of polychromatic blue‐enriching evening room light on sleep is not as straightforward as previously suggested.
exposure to light in the short wavelength spectrum may have an acute impact on sleep regulation in humans, and this should be taken into consideration in the development of new lighting technologies.

blue‐enriching light at relatively low levels may be a promising strategy to improve alertness and cognitive function, and may also be used as a countermeasure against the negative effects of blue‐enlightening light on human circadian rhythms and sleep quality.
